1:
The shadow is the first question, and Calvin and Robertson take it oppositely. Robertson makes the contrast one between a shade cast by interrupted light and a painted likeness, reading the verse alongside Colossians 2:17, where shadow stands against body; the law gives only a dim outline. Calvin expressly separates the two texts. There the rites are shadows because they lack the substance; here the figure is from the painter's craft, the rude lineaments sketched before the living colours are laid on, so the difference between law and gospel is between an outline and a finished picture. Ellicott finds the antithesis surprising, since image means only a likeness and not the things themselves, and answers that the law could not be conceived as possessing the good things, though a representation as perfect as the very image might have carried equal efficacy. Gill limits it to the ceremonial law, the moral law being neither obscure nor transitory; Henry asks who would dote upon a shadow, however good, once the substance has come.

The argument from repetition is put most vividly by Barnes, who compares the offerings to medicine: what heals need not be given twice, and a remedy taken all a man's life while the disease remains proves insufficient. Ellicott says the same in a phrase, that the very repetition testified to imperfection, and corrects the rendering so that worshippers once cleansed would have had no more consciousness of sins; Robertson insists on the same word. Clarke grants the logic and then observes what the practice shows: no Jew pretended the annual atonement cancelled his sin before God, yet he kept offering because the law required it and the sacrifices pointed forward. Gill records that several versions drop the negative, the sense requiring that or the clause read as a question.

On the yearly remembrance Ellicott supplies the detail that in each of his three prayers the high priest acknowledged sin by name, for himself and his house, for the priesthood, and for a people gone perversely. Robertson notes the word is simply a reminder, the one used at the supper; Wesley calls it a public commemoration of the sins of the last year and all before it, clear proof that the guilt was not purged away. Calvin turns the verse into an argument, then a weapon. The remembrance meant is not any recollection but the sort that confesses guilt and so requires a sacrifice for its removal; and if the writer concludes the legal sacrifices were weak because repeated every year, then by the same reasoning a sacrifice offered daily to apply its virtue would be weak too, whatever masks are put upon it.

The impossibility stated at the end is taken as the ground of everything before it. Barnes says the blood of an animal had no power to wash away a moral offence, to repair the law, or to make the heart pure; Clarke thinks common sense must have taught them as much, and that God intended them to understand it. Ellicott balances the two sides: the offering was necessary and answered its purpose, but could not remove the need of another and better one. Calvin supplies the contrast the writer leaves unspoken: the Jews had in that blood a symbol and pledge of the real cleansing, but the argument concerns what the blood of beasts could do in itself, and Christ's offering is not to be measured by it. Cyril reaches it from the other end, quoting the passage about the greater tabernacle and the eternal redemption to seal the cry that it is finished and sins are forgiven. Wesley draws the sharpest consequence: if the law was a bare unsubstantial shadow, how can anyone take the attainments of David, or of any man under that dispensation, for the measure of gospel holiness, as though Christian experience were to rise no higher than Jewish.
5:
The moment of the coming is disputed mildly. Barnes reports the question whether the words belong to the birth or to the entrance on the ministry, notes that Grotius took the second, and declines to decide since nothing turns on it. Calvin makes it the manifestation in the flesh, when he put on man's nature to be a Redeemer, as elsewhere he is said to have come down from heaven. Gill clears away three other readings, the coming into Judea, the passage from private life into public, and the entrance into the world to come which a Targum supplies, dismissed because the other world is never called simply the world. Wesley makes the best of the phrase: into the world and not into the tabernacle, because the whole world has an interest in this sacrifice.

The quotation itself diverges from the Hebrew at its most famous point. Clarke sets the two side by side: the Greek reads that a body was prepared, while David wrote that his ears were opened, or rather bored, the mark of the servant made his master's for ever and kept in his house. Robertson defends the substitution, holding that the Greek has not altered the sense, since the ears were the point of contact with God's will, and that the argument stands either way, the Son's offering being the sacrifice prophecy said God desired. Ellicott agrees the version followed is faithful on the whole, one clause only presenting difficulty, and flags a word of some importance dropped from the verse that follows. Clarke ties the prepared body to the conception, and so to the promise about the seed of the woman.

Whose psalm it is divides them sharply. Gill denies it can be David's words about himself, and gives reasons: sacrifice was still required in his day, he could not fulfil the law, he never engaged as surety, and nothing was written of him in the volume of the book; the speaker is one not yet come though ready to come. Calvin takes the opposite ground, that the whole psalm accords with David, and meets the obvious objection himself, since the confession that his iniquities had laid hold on him suits Christ only as he took on himself the sins of his members; David being a type, there is nothing unreasonable in transferring to Christ what David said of himself, least of all where the abolishing of the ceremonies is in question. Ellicott stands nearer Calvin, thinking the psalm probably David's as the inscription says, and places it with a small group remarkable for anticipating the prophets on the inferior worth of ceremony beside moral duty. Calvin adds that not everyone reads the clause as repudiating sacrifice at all, some taking it to strike only at the notion that worship consisted in it.

On the want of pleasure the difference is one of degree, but real. Barnes points out that the words are not quoted literally, one Greek word being changed, and reads the sense comparatively, that God had no pleasure in the offerings as against obedience, adding that when made with a pure heart they doubtless pleased him. Clarke allows nothing of the kind: God could never be pleased with the victims under the law, nor consider them atonements for sin, since they could neither satisfy his justice nor make his law honourable. Ellicott corrects the rendering to whole burnt offerings, the symbol of entire consecration, mentioned in the Epistle only here and three verses later, and brings the tense back to the past. Robertson names the four offerings the psalm sets aside: the animal sacrifice, the meal offering, the whole burnt offering and the offering concerning sin. Barnes closes where the argument needs it: such offerings were never what was required of the one now speaking, whose end could be reached only by obedience unto death.
7:
What book is meant divides them four ways. Clarke says the roll must be the Pentateuch, since in David's time no other part of revelation had been written, and explains the word from the practice of writing on skins wound between two rollers, which gave the Romans their name for a volume. Wesley narrows it to the psalm in hand. Henry keeps it broad, that God had not only decreed but declared by Moses and the prophets that Christ should come. Robertson widens it to the older Scriptures taken as a prediction of the higher sacrifice, the Greek word being a diminutive meaning a little head and so a roll. Calvin proposes another sense: while the Law may be understood, he thinks it likelier that the speaker means he found himself in the catalogue of those called to obey God, and testified that he answered the call. Ellicott sets out two renderings of the Hebrew, one making the roll prescribe the coming, the other making the speaker come with the roll, and observes that dropping the words I delight alters the connection while preserving the sense.

Chrysostom alone names the objection the argument is answering. If the sacrifices were types, someone will ask, how is it that after the truth has come they have not ceased nor given place but are still performed? He answers that the writer labours at exactly this point, showing that they are no longer performed even as a figure because God does not accept them, and showing it out of the prophets rather than the newer books, with the strongest testimony from times of old. Ellicott finds the same purpose in a small change of wording, the offerings being described as made according to law rather than according to the law, as if the contrast were between any external ritual and a principle of inward obedience.

On what is taken away and what established, Barnes and Robertson agree that the first is the system of animal sacrifice and the second the doing of God's will, Robertson calling the sentence the writer's own exposition of the psalm. Clarke lists the alternatives, first covenant and second, first dispensation and second, law and gospel, judges the sense nearly the same and prefers the plainest. Ellicott asks how the removal worked twice over, for the psalmist and then for Christ. David, seeing that what God seeks is the subjection of a man's will, refuses to rest in the sacrifices; yet nobody supposes burnt offering was at an end for him, since his own confession of iniquity implied recourse to the appointed means, and the sacrifices were taken up into the service of obedience. Calvin puts it positively, that when the legal sacrifices are removed the will of God stands as a perfect rule, and is careful to say what is not condemned: not hypocrisy, not superstitious worship, but the claim that such sacrifices are still required of a rightly instructed man.

The sanctifying is referred by all to the offering rather than to obedience in general. Barnes is explicit that it was not merely doing God's will at large but the particular thing of offering his body in place of the Jewish sacrifices, and warns that the word is not confined here to what is usually called sanctification. Gill distinguishes three senses in which the offering was God's will, of purpose, of command, and of good pleasure. Calvin extends the passage beyond its head, since readiness to do God's will belongs to all Christ's members, sanctification being God's general will for them, though the offering on the cross was a supereminent instance. Clarke draws the consequence in order, that the will of God is the incarnation, the death, the tasting of death for every man, and the believing of all who will; Wesley states the result in five words, cleansed from guilt and consecrated to God.
11:
The contrast of posture is what all notice. Clarke sets the standing servant at the altar against the Son seated at the right hand and makes the point turn on it: the continual offering argued imperfection, the single offering proves completeness. Wesley says the standing is a servant's humble posture; Robertson calls the participles a graphic picture of the priest at work. Barnes guards the detail, that not every priest served daily, since they went by courses, only that the thing was done each day. Calvin draws the conclusion of the whole argument, that daily sacrificing is wholly foreign to Christ's priesthood, so the Levitical priests were deposed by his coming, since when one of two contraries is set up the other falls.

Two small questions follow. Barnes points out that the word man is not in the Greek, which says only this one, and states nothing about his nature; Ellicott renders it simply but He. Then a real ambiguity of punctuation: the words for ever may be joined to the offering before them or the sitting down after, and Ellicott observes that the editions of the English Bible and Prayer Book are divided, while Robertson allows both. Wesley takes the first, that the virtue of the one sacrifice remains for ever. On the waiting Ellicott catches a reversal: earlier the thought was of a coming for those who wait for him; here it is he who waits. Robertson calls the attitude one of final and certain victory; Clarke hears an oblique reference to the fall of Jerusalem then at hand. Cyril gathers the testimonies to the session out of Matthew, Peter and Paul.

The next sentence sets a completed act beside a continuing one, and Robertson marks the grammar: he has perfected stands in the perfect, those who are sanctified in the present, either because the process is still going forward or because it is repeated in so many persons. Ellicott recalls that perfection came neither by the Levitical priesthood nor by the law, and that what all priestly service aimed at is at last reached. The prophecy is then quoted a second time, and Calvin explains why it is not superfluous: the first citation showed that the old covenant had to be abrogated because a new one was promised, and this serves another purpose. Gill draws a chain of doctrine from the bare preface: the Spirit witnesses in the Old Testament books and is therefore their author, existed then, is truly God and a distinct person. Clarke says more simply that we are assured Jeremiah spoke by inspiration. Wesley calls it a winding-up of the argument, the covenant now completely ratified.

The way the quotation is handled draws careful notice. Ellicott and Robertson agree the writer is not aiming at verbal agreement, since the opening lines are dropped, later lines omitted, the house of Israel replaced by a pronoun, heart and mind reversed, and iniquities added to sins. Ellicott then says what most readers feel, that as the verses stand in the Authorised version the sense is imperfect, since the words about what was said before require a then he saith somewhere after, which the translators did not supply, the marginal note offering it having been added later. The close is agreed. Barnes says that where sins are blotted out there is no more need of a sacrifice than of paying a debt twice; Clarke reports the same argument turned against the mass; Robertson calls it the triumphant conclusion, and Ellicott marks it as the end of the argument and the start of the Epistle's last division, which alternates encouragement with warning. Henry states the gain in a sentence: under the old covenant sacrifices had to be repeated and secured pardon only as to this world, while under the new one sacrifice procures for all nations and ages freedom from punishment in the world to come.
19:
All mark the turn. Barnes says the hortatory part begins here and runs to the end; Clarke that the doctrine being finished, the writer now shows what influence it should have on hearts and lives; Wesley calls the opening a brief recapitulation. Robertson counts it the second summary of the five arguments about the priestly work, joined to an exhortation like the one that opened the discussion; Ellicott notes the same likeness and explains the greater fulness by the growth of the thought. Chrysostom recites the differences established, of High Priest and sacrifice and tabernacle and covenant and promise, and puts the contrast in four pairs: temporal and eternal, near vanishing and permanent, powerless and perfect, figure and reality.

The boldness is read as the note of the whole letter. Robertson says it is the dominant note throughout and the need of the hour, these readers being tempted to give up Christ and quit. Clarke measures it against the old rite: the high priest went in with fear and trembling, knowing that neglect of the least prescribed thing meant death. Henry unfolds what the privilege contains: access to God, light to direct, liberty of spirit and speech, a right to it and a readiness for it, help to use it and assurance of acceptance. Ellicott corrects the preposition to in the blood rather than by it, and denies that any comparison is drawn between Christ's people and the Jewish high priest, since we do not enter carrying blood as he did; as the whole people symbolically entered with him when he passed the veil, so we enter with our own High Priest, who went in by his own blood. Calvin defends the figure, granting that allegories sometimes obscure a subject rather than illustrate it, but holding that when the ancient shapes of the Law are transferred to Christ there is no small elegance and no small light in them.

On the new way they converge, and the detail is worth having. Barnes notes that the word rendered new occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and properly means freshly killed, so its force is recent rather than unprecedented; he reports Doddridge, following Owen, rendering it an ever living way. Clarke presses the same sense into the practice: only blood still warm and fluid served for sprinkling, and once it cooled and thickened it was unfit, so Christ is figured as newly slain and yet living, his blood always flowing and giving life. Gill enters a qualification the others do not, that the way is not new in contrivance or revelation or use, having been planned before the world and shown to our first parents, but new against the old way of life by works and newly revealed with greater clearness; he takes living against the dead carcasses of beasts and the dead letter of the law.

The veil divides them, and the division is instructive. Calvin makes the flesh a covering: as the veil hid the recesses of the sanctuary and yet gave entrance, so the divinity hidden in Christ's flesh leads us into heaven, and no one finds God but the man to whom the man Christ becomes the door; from which he draws two rules: Christ's glory is not measured by the outward appearance of his flesh, and his flesh is not to be despised, since what conceals the majesty of God also conducts us to all his good. Wesley takes it the other way: as the rending of the temple veil made the holiest visible and accessible, so the wounding of Christ's body manifested the God of heaven and opened the way. Robertson reports both readings, that the veil is the humanity through which God is revealed and that some take it for what obscured his deity, and settles for the first. Gill keeps to the way itself, that all who walk in it live.
21:
Gill, Ellicott and Robertson all observe that the Greek says a great priest rather than a high priest, and Ellicott alone explains the change: the phrase is a standing name for the high priest in Hebrew and Greek alike, and its appearance after so many chapters of the other word suggests that Zechariah's prophecy about the crowning of Joshua, which unites priestly and kingly imagery, was before the writer's mind. On the house they agree it is the church. Clarke presses the parallel of office, that as the high priest ordered everything belonging to the house and the worship, so does Christ in the government of his Church, and adds the corollary that this government he never put into other hands, since none can save the Church but the Lord Jesus, as none can preserve the world but God. Calvin gives the purpose of the appointment: whoever seeks a place in the Church must submit to Christ and choose him, and no other, for leader and ruler.

Robertson notes the structure, three exhortations in as many verses, to draw near, to hold fast and to consider one another. On the drawing near Gill and Ellicott take the language as priestly: it is a sacerdotal act belonging to all the saints, who are themselves made priests, and it is as priests, sprinkled with the blood of atonement, that they enter the house. On the fulness of faith Barnes makes it an unwavering confidence leaving no room for doubt, Clarke a full persuasion that God will accept us for his Son's sake, Ellicott a counterpart to the fulness of hope named earlier. On the sprinkling Clarke marks the contrast, that not the body is sprinkled as the Hebrews were but the heart, cleansed by the blood; Wesley reads the washing of the body as a spotless conversation, more acceptable than all the legal washings; Calvin puts the rule behind both, that since nothing in Christ's sacrifice is other than spiritual, what we bring must correspond.

The next exhortation turns on a word the English Bible gets wrong. Ellicott states it plainly: the rendering profession of our faith is found in no earlier English version and is supposed an oversight of the translators, the true reading being the hope; and the words that follow belong to the confession, so the sense is to hold fast the confession of the hope so that it does not waver. Clarke reports the same reading among many variants; Robertson says simply that it is a confession of hope, not of despair. Calvin explains why hope is named rather than faith, hope being born of faith and then feeding and sustaining it to the end; he insists on the confession because faith is not true unless it shows itself before men, and thinks the writer glances at those who attended too carefully to the ceremonies to please their own nation. Wesley identifies the hope as the one professed at baptism.

The last of the three moves from the individual to the body, as Ellicott observes, and he suspects a reason, that among these readers there had been provocations that did not tend to brotherly love; the strict sense may be no more than taking note of one another, while the converse is included in the result, that we should be so provoked ourselves. Robertson notes that the word gives us paroxysm and means to sharpen or incite, used here in a good sense though elsewhere of irritation; Barnes makes the same point from the English side, that provoke now means to offend; Clarke supports the favourable sense from Xenophon, who says Cyrus by praises and gifts excited his officers as much as he could. Calvin thinks the Jews specially addressed, the arrogance of that nation being notorious, boasting itself alone chosen, despising others and superciliously claiming to be the Church, a pride the apostles laboured much to correct.
25:
Three of them find the same thing in the compound word. Calvin points out that the prefix signifies an addition, so the noun means a congregation enlarged by newcomers: the partition wall being pulled down, God was gathering as children those who had been aliens, and the Gentiles were an unwonted addition which the Jews felt as a reproach, so many seceded on the ground that such a mixture excused them. Gill says the same in a phrase: the word distinguishes Christian assemblies from Jewish synagogues and marks the coalition of Jews and Gentiles in one church. Ellicott observes that the Greek alludes to the technical name of the synagogue while avoiding it, and thinks some had persuaded themselves that the older religion's relation to the newer let them keep clear of Christian assemblies; that neglect, he says, was the first step toward apostasy. On what meeting is meant, Barnes rejects the view that the church as a society is intended and prefers public worship; Clarke thinks private meetings likelier, the church being under persecution; Wesley allows either.

Why some stayed away is variously guessed. Clarke ascribes it to fear of persecution, and warns that those giving up the strengthening means put others in danger; Wesley adds a vain imagination of being above external ordinances; Robertson notes drily that some had already formed the habit of absence, perilous then and now. Over the day that draws near they divide. Clarke takes it of the judgments about to fall on the Jewish nation, Ellicott of the Son of Man coming in judgment on Jerusalem, Robertson of the Second Coming, drawing nearer all the time; Wesley leaves it the great day, ever to be kept in view.

The warning is defined chiefly by what it excludes. Gill says it is not a single act, nor sins of infirmity, nor even grosser acts of sin, but what is done on set purpose, resolutely and obstinately, not immoral practices but corrupt principles acted on, amounting to total apostasy against light. Ellicott puts it grammatically: the case is not if we fall under temptation and commit sin, but if we are sinning wilfully, a continued state expressing apostasy, and the knowledge received is not knowledge merely but full knowledge, as Robertson also insists. Clarke says flatly that the passage has nothing to do with backsliders in the common sense, but describes a deliberate apostate who has rejected the atonement and renounced the gospel. Barnes defends the same reading with numbered arguments: it is the natural sense, which would occur to ninety-nine readers in a hundred if no theory had to be protected; it accords with the scope of a letter written to keep readers from going back; and it fits the fair meaning of the words.

Calvin adds the history of the verse's misuse, the most useful thing said about it. An early sect armed itself with this testimony to deny pardon to all who had fallen after baptism, and those who could not refute the calumny chose rather to deny the Epistle's authority than grant so great an absurdity. The remedy, he says, is the passage itself, which condemns not those who offend in some way but those who forsake the Church and wholly alienate themselves. Chrysostom sets the threat in a figure: trees planted and tended and watered which yield nothing are pulled up and given to the fire; the writer, having urged from the kindlier considerations, now urges from the gloomier. Henry describes the sin as a total falling away in which men with fixed will reject the only Saviour, resist the only Sanctifier and renounce the only gospel; he asks what could be sorer than dying without mercy and answers that one thing is, to die by mercy, by the very grace despised; but he adds that none of it means a soul which sorrows for sin will be shut out.
27:
Barnes begins by removing a word: the English certain does not mean fixed or inevitable, since the Greek says only a fearful expectation, and he notes that Tindale had it right. Robertson adds that the noun usually means reception or interpretation, and that this sense looks coined by the writer. Ellicott renders it a fearful awaiting of judgment and a jealousy of fire that shall devour the adversaries, traces the second half to an adaptation of Isaiah, and draws the antithesis that gives the verse its force: for Christ's waiting servants the thought of judgment is swallowed up in salvation, while for these nothing is left but the awaiting of judgment. Clarke glosses the phrase as a fervour of fire like that which fell on Korah, and thinks the unbelieving nation and the burning of their city are in view. Calvin locates the terror inwardly, in the torment of a conscience that not only lacks grace but knows it tasted grace and lost it by its own fault; such men war rebelliously against God because they cannot endure so strict a Judge, and try every way in vain to shake off the sense of his wrath.

The comparison that follows is a standard form, and Robertson names it: an argument from the less to the greater, the first of Hillel's seven rules. Ellicott identifies the law in question as the passage in Deuteronomy about apostasy to idols, and draws the point: the sin which by everyone's admission once robbed Israel of the name of God's people is set silently beside the sin of those who forsake Christ. Barnes guards the statement, that not every offender under Moses died without mercy but only where the offence was capital, apostasy being such a case; Wesley says the same in three words. Clarke defines the despising as rejection and denial of divine authority by presumptuous sin. Calvin observes that this reasoning was peculiarly fitted to Jewish readers, since so severe a penalty on apostates under the Law was neither new nor could seem unjustly rigorous, so they were bound to grant the justice of the heavier vengeance; the version, he adds, should read rejected rather than despised.

Calvin counts three charges in the description of desertion, that the Son of God is trodden under foot, his blood reckoned unholy, and despite done to the Spirit of grace; and he weighs them, since treading under foot is more heinous than despising, and the dignity of Christ is of another order than that of Moses. Wesley makes the same comparison in a phrase, a lawgiver far more honourable than Moses. Ellicott presses the middle charge: the blood by which the covenant was established, in which the man had received a sanctification the law could not give, he has esteemed an unholy thing; and there is no middle ground between highest reverence and utter contumely. Clarke reads the word for unholy as common, meaning they expected nothing from that blood by way of atonement, and asks how near the same ruin men come today who reject the atoning blood.

Two consequences are drawn. Barnes argues that the punishment must be future, since the severest penalty the older law could inflict was death and something worse is here deserved; and he rests it on God's justice, that if such a man ought to be so regarded he will be. Wesley draws the other consequence from the clause about the blood by which the apostate was sanctified: Christ died for him also, and he was at least justified once. Gill keeps the contrast narrow, the sorer punishment being sorer than the bodily death the law of Moses inflicted. Cyril, expounding the dignity here trampled, asks by what sign the promised King is known, since purple and spearmen and a golden chariot have all been anticipated by other kings, and demands a mark belonging to this one alone.
30:
The quotation raises a question of form and a question of use. Ellicott observes that it keeps the sense of the Hebrew while departing from its wording, and that the Greek version diverges further by losing the emphasis on the words to me; what he finds remarkable is that the citation appears in this exact form in Romans, and since an ancient Targum has the phrase I will recompense, he suggests a rendering already current was taken up. Barnes points out that the same words serve in Romans to forbid private revenge and here to promise certain punishment; Calvin notices the difficulty more sharply, since in Moses the promise is that God will avenge wrongs done to his people, a strained fit for the vengeance meant here, so the two applications must be distinguished. On the second clause they part outright: Clarke reads it as executing judgment on his people's behalf, plainly the sense of the passage quoted, while Wesley reads it as judging them, far more rigorously than the heathen if they rebel.

The sentence about falling into God's hands is glossed from several directions. Gill turns the phrase over: in one sense all men are in God's hands, believers especially, whose persons and times are there, and who would rather fall into a chastising Father's hands than into men's; but that is not the sense here. Clarke presses the adjective, that he who lives for ever can punish for ever, so that the displeasure rests not for a time but through eternity. Ellicott points out that the Greek says a living God, and that the chapter of Deuteronomy still in view supplies the reason, God there lifting his hand to heaven and saying that he lives for ever. Robertson refuses to soften it: we are not dealing with a dead or absentee God but with one alive and alert.

Then the tone changes, and Chrysostom explains the change by a figure. The best physicians, having made a deep incision and increased the pain by the wound, do not cut a second time but soothe what they have opened with gentle remedies; so here, after shaking his readers with the recollection of hell and convincing them that the man who does despite to grace must perish, the writer turns to what will give rest. Ellicott marks the same turn from warning to encouragement, and quotes the remark that he bids them imitate not others but themselves. Calvin explains why the memory is useful: it is shameful to begin well and faint midway, more shameful to go backward after real progress, so the remembrance of past warfare serves not as a pretext for sloth, as though one had served his time, but to make a man more active in finishing his course.

The trials are described in the language of the games. Clarke renders the phrase a great combat or contention of sufferings and hears an allusion to the Grecian contests; Robertson derives the noun from the verb for competing in public games. On the exposure they differ: Clarke takes it literally, that they were exhibited like wild beasts at the theatres, Ellicott thinks the word probably figurative, and Barnes leaves it open, saying only that they were held up to public scorn. Clarke admires those who did not suffer directly, since when a victim was marked out the rest were prompt to take his part and own the same faith, where many would have slunk into a corner; Ellicott makes them not companions merely but sharers, by sympathy and voluntary association; Henry generalises it, that the Christian spirit is not selfish but puts us on pitying others, visiting and helping and pleading for them. Calvin draws the warning: since men whose faith had been proved by no common trials still needed urging forward, none should flatter himself that he has reached the goal.
34:
The verse opens on a textual question that changes who is being pitied. Gill notes that the Alexandrian copy and the Vulgate and Syriac read had compassion on them that were bound, meaning prisoners generally, or those imprisoned for the Gospel. Clarke reports the same variant from two uncials and several versions and Greek fathers, so well supported that Griesbach admitted it into the text, and infers that several were then bound for the testimony of Jesus, whom the Judean church openly owned and relieved. Ellicott treats it as the true reading outright and adds that the change is very important in connection with the question of authorship. Robertson renders it with the prisoners. Calvin declines to decide: the manuscript authority is nearly equal and the context undecisive; what he does notice is an inversion, the last subject of the preceding verse being taken up first here. Barnes keeps the first person and builds on it, placing the imprisonment at Caesarea (Acts 24:27), where friends had free access.

On the plunder itself they agree in substance and differ in emphasis. Clarke grades it: to suffer such persecution patiently was great, to endure it without a murmur greater, to rejoice in it greatest of all. Calvin refuses to make the joy a denial of grief, since poverty considered in itself touched them with sorrow; but as they looked higher they found a cause of joy that allayed it, and they were fixed on the recompense rather than glad to be plundered. Barnes states it as a fact about human nature: men may be brought to part with their property with joy; it is not usually the case, but religion will do it. Ellicott sets the temper beside the beatitude of Matthew 5:12, that they accepted persecution not with patience and long suffering only but with joy.

The last clause divides them more sharply, because Ellicott's text differs from theirs. He removes in heaven as a comment absent from the oldest manuscripts, prefers the reading yourselves, and translates: perceiving that ye have your own selves for a better possession and one that abideth, the lesson of the saying about the man who gains the world and loses himself. The others expound the heavenly inheritance the words seem to name. Barnes makes the comparison quantitative, the treasure laid up there worth more than all the wealth of Croesus. Clarke asks how they could bear the loss and answers from this clause: they had the fullest evidence of being God's children, the Spirit bearing witness, and if children then heirs. Wesley compresses the verse into one sentence: they sympathised with all their suffering brethren and received joyfully the loss of their goods.

The exhortation that follows is military. Clarke hears in cast not away a reference to cowardly soldiers who throw away their shields and run, and quotes what Spartan women said in handing one over, either bring this back or be brought back upon it. Barnes reaches the same figure from Rosenmuller and documents the disgrace, capital among the Greeks, and among the Germans on Tacitus's account so deep that many who lost the shield ended their lives with the halter. Robertson keeps to the verb, used elsewhere in the New Testament only of Bartimaeus throwing off his garment, and names the danger plainly: these readers were in peril of a panic and of a stampede away from Christ. Gill takes the noun three ways, as boldness in prayer free of a servile spirit, as open profession, or as assurance of interest in God, none of which should be slackened. On the patience required Calvin argues that Christians will never advance two paces without fainting unless patience sustains them against the adversary's endless devices; Clarke divides the labour, God furnishing the grace and the man exercising it, so that here we are workers together with God.
37:
The closing quotation is composite, and two of the commentators say so. Robertson observes that the opening words come from Isaiah 26:20 as an introduction to the passage taken from Habakkuk, and that the article prefixed to he that cometh is an addition to the prophet, giving the phrase a Messianic application. Ellicott makes the same identification and presses it: the expression is remarkable and unusual, and the passage it is borrowed from is about the Lord coming to punish the inhabitants of the earth, so that even the passing echo would raise those associations for Hebrew readers. Calvin sees the same freedom differently, noting that the writer follows the Greek version and so departs somewhat from the prophet's words, and he explains the purpose of the reminder by a comparison: as a general holds out to his soldiers the prospect that the war will soon end if they hold out a little longer, so believers are told the deliverance is near.

What coming is meant divides them. Gill rules out the coming in the flesh, since that had already happened, and takes it of Christ coming in kingdom and power to destroy Jerusalem and avenge his rejection. Clarke says the same more bluntly, that in a very short time the Messiah would execute judgment on their rebellious country, and adds that the apostle accommodates the prophet's words to his own purpose. Barnes hesitates between an allusion to the Lord's own a little while and the Habakkuk passage, but settles on the same destruction of the Jewish power. Wesley reads the clause quite otherwise, glossing he that cometh as coming to reward every man according to his works, which puts the reference at the last judgment rather than at the fall of the city.

On the next clause Ellicott alone works from the text upward. The Greek is not perfectly certain, he says, but the word my should probably be added, giving but my righteous one shall live by faith; the Hebrew reads altogether differently, opening with a description of the haughty invader, and the Greek copies differ among themselves in the order of the two halves. The others take the clause as it stands and expound it. Calvin makes patience the child of faith, since it is by faith that we leap over the perils and miseries of this life and keep a quiet standing in storms, and he reads the future tense as marking the perpetuity of that life. Barnes gives it a practical turn: the righteous are to pass their lives not in doubt and fear and trembling apprehension but in calm trust. Gill narrows the life meant, denying that eternal life is in view and identifying a present life of justification, communion and holiness.

Then comes the sharpest exchange in the chapter. Clarke insists that the one who may draw back is the justified man himself, the relative having no other antecedent, and calls the inserted words any man a wicked perversion of the words of God if done to serve a particular creed, since their effect is to save the doctrine of final and unconditional perseverance. Wesley agrees, taking the drawing back as shipwreck of faith and the following clause as outright rejection. Gill answers by distinguishing: there is a drawing back that is not unto perdition, and David and Peter are the instances, but the total and final sort cannot happen to true believers, who are held by everlasting love. Barnes takes a third line, that the case is only supposable, stated as a general principle of the divine administration precisely in order to keep them from it. Robertson stays with the vocabulary, the noun meaning stealthy retreat in Plutarch and dissimulation in Josephus, while Clarke renders the last verse as a contrast of character: we are not the cowards, but the courageous.
